title: SQL Injection in product search endpoint
description: The /products/search endpoint concatenates the user-supplied 'q' query parameter directly into a SQL string without using parameterized queries. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL to read, modify, or delete data, or potentially execute OS commands via SQLite extensions.
evidence: Line 41: "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%'" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%'" + q + "%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 50". Tested with GET /products/search?q=' OR 1=1-- which returned all products instead of zero results.

title: SQL Injection in admin reviews-by-customer endpoint
description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint embeds customer['display_name'] directly into a SQL query string via f-string interpolation. Since display_name is stored in the database and controlled by users (set during registration), an authenticated admin can be tricked into querying against malicious input, but more critically, if any external party could influence display_name prior to this query, it would be exploitable. In practice, since only staff can access this, the risk is lower, but the injection vector is present.
evidence: Line 80: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'". Tested with a crafted display_name containing a quote character causing SQL errors.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery via pickle deserialization in basket cookie
description: The basket cookie stores Python objects serialized with pickle, then unpickled server-side in read_basket(). While there is a try/except around pickle.loads(), an attacker who can craft a malicious pickle payload can achieve remote code execution when the server deserializes it. The cookie is sent with every request.
evidence: Lines 19-21: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) inside read_basket(). Pickle deserialization is inherently unsafe as it executes arbitrary Python code from the deserialized object.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery via pickle deserialization in cache files
description: The cache module uses pickle to serialize and deserialize cached data files on disk. If an attacker can write to the cache directory (or if the filesystem is compromised), they can plant malicious pickle payloads that will be executed upon cache reads. The CACHE_DIR permissions are set to 0700 but within the same process, path traversal or other attacks could compromise safety.
evidence: Line 23: pickle.load(f) inside get(). Line 31: pickle.dump(value, f) inside put(). Deserialization of potentially tampered data.

title: Token refresh endpoint bypasses signature verification
description: The /auth/refresh endpoint calls jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}), which accepts any JWT regardless of its signature. An attacker can forge tokens with arbitrary claims (including role: 'staff') to gain authentication and escalate privileges. This completely undermines the security of the session management system.
evidence: Line 101: jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}). Verified with POST /auth/refresh using a forged token - the server accepted it and returned a fresh valid token for sub=1 with role='customer'.

title: Hardcoded secret key
description: The SECRET_KEY used for signing JWT tokens is hardcoded as a static string 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'. This means anyone with access to the source code can forge valid JWT tokens for any user, including admin/staff accounts. It also weakens defense in depth if the token-refresh vulnerability is patched.
evidence: Line 3: SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'. This key is used in make_token() and user_from_request() for JWT encoding/decoding.

title: Default webhook secret is easily guessable
description: WEBHOOK_SECRET defaults to 'whsec-local', a trivially guessable value. While it can be overridden via environment variable, running with the default exposes the application to webhook forgery - an attacker can craft fake payment webhook events that pass signature verification, potentially marking unpaid orders as paid.
evidence: Line 8: WEBHOOK_SECRET = os.environ.get('WEBHOOK_SECRET', 'whsec-local'). See payments.py webhook_signature() which uses this to verify incoming webhooks.

title: Incorrect HMAC API usage in webhook signature verification
description: The webhook_signature function uses hmac.new() (with lowercase 'new') instead of hmac.new() -- actually, Python's standard library module is 'hmac' and the function is hmac.new(). However, looking at line 55: hmac.new(secret, str(order_id).encode(), hashlib.sha256). The correct API should use hmac.new() but the actual function name in the hmac module is hmac.new()... wait - the issue is that it uses hmac.new() but the correct function call should use hashlib.sha256 as the digestfunc argument correctly, BUT the real problem is: hmac.new() takes three arguments where the third is the hash function. Actually 'hmac.new()' IS the correct function. The issue here may not be real.
evidence: Need to re-examine this - hmac.new() is actually the correct Python API. The function name is 'new' not 'new'. Actually let me reconsider: in Python the function is indeed hmac.new(secret, msg, digestmod). So this is NOT a finding. Removing.

title: CORS configured to reflect any origin with credentials
description: The CORS handler in __init__.py sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the value of the requesting Origin header unconditionally, and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to 'true'. This allows any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to the application, enabling cross-site request forgery attacks from malicious third-party sites.
evidence: Lines 44-51 in __init__.py: resp.headers['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = origin with no allowlist check, combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

title: Request body logged for POST/PUT/PATCH requests
description: The before_request hook logs the full request body for POST, PUT, and PATCH requests up to 2000 characters. If these requests contain sensitive data like passwords, tokens, or personal information, that data will appear in logs. For example, /auth/register and /auth/login send password fields that would be logged.
evidence: Lines 29-31 in __init__.py: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000])

title: Debug mode enabled in application start script
description: The run.py script starts Flask with debug=True. In debug mode, Flask provides an interactive debugger that can be triggered by certain error pages. An attacker could potentially exploit this to execute arbitrary code if they can trigger an exception in the application.

title: Weak password hashing using plain SHA-256 without salt
description: Passwords are hashed using plain SHA-256 without a per-password salt. This makes passwords vulnerable to rainbow table attacks and precomputation attacks. Additionally, SHA-256 is too fast for password hashing; slow hashes like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 should be used.
evidence: Line 16: return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() in hash_password(). No salt is used.

title: Reset token uses cryptographically weak randomness
description: Password reset tokens are generated using random.random() which produces a float between 0 and 1 with limited precision, then formatted as an 8-digit decimal. This creates only 10^8 possible values, making brute-force recovery of the token feasible.
evidence: Line 135: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8). Only 100 million possible tokens, generated using non-cryptographic random.

title: Order detail view missing ownership check
description: The /orders/<int:order_id> endpoint returns full order details to any authenticated user without verifying that the order belongs to them. While own_order() checks ownership for cancellations and returns, show_order() uses get_order() which only checks existence, not ownership. This allows any authenticated user to view other users' orders.
evidence: Line 49: Returns order_json(get_order(order_id)) without checking g.user['id'] matches order['customer_id']. Verified: User 1 can see User 2's order by forging JWT with sub=2, and also Order 2 visible without auth restrictions beyond general login requirement.

title: Editable package install without checksum verification
description: requirements-dev.txt installs hf-payments as an editable package (-e packages/hf_payments) without any dependency hash or pinning verification. Combined with requirements.txt pulling from an internal PyPI index (pypi.hartleyfinch.internal), this means that if the internal index or hf-payments source is compromised, arbitrary code can be injected into the build.
evidence: Line 6 of requirements-dev.txt: -e packages/hf_payments. The pyproject.toml has no constraints on dependencies and pip editable installs don't verify checksums.
